summary:
Dancing with the SARs is an open, browser-based 3D globe that makes Earth’s changing surface understandable through NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations. It combines satellite imagery with live earthquake, wildfire, flood and storm reports from USGS, NASA EONET and GDACS, letting users explore available radar passes before and after events.
At selected places, calibrated measurements identify where radar echoes differ from their earlier observations. Following an October 2026 flood in Tuscany, 3.5% of the analysed cells stood out three days after the event, compared with none on the preceding pass; where nothing happened, the same test flags 0.06%. Over Bardhaman in West Bengal, measurements follow a rice-growing season from flooded paddies to harvest.
We address the challenge through interactive change maps, time series and animations, comparing radar polarisations and labelling possible physical explanations as hypotheses rather than proven causes.
Radar can observe through clouds, smoke and darkness when optical views are obscured. By translating these observations into accessible visualisations with linked sources and explicit limitations, our app helps non-specialists explore changes relevant to disasters, agriculture and the environment. Every number shown is computed from the data, and it requires no login or installation.
details:
1. WHAT IT DOES
Dancing with the SARs is an interactive, browser-based 3D globe that shows Earth’s changing surface through NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations. It combines a global radar view with earthquake, wildfire, flood and storm reports from USGS, NASA EONET and GDACS. Each event opens on a timeline with available satellite passes before and after it. Users can drag through observations, compare images, or search a location to explore its radar history. Five stories and 33 “changing places” explain slower changes in glaciers, wetlands, sinking cities, forests and farmland.

2. HOW IT WORKS
Our Python pipeline reads NISAR’s calibrated backscatter measurements from L2 GCOV products, analysing the ground in 500-metre cells. A detector identifies cells that differ from both their recent observations and longer history, using HH and HV polarisations together where available. Only spatial clusters count, and open water is excluded.

Following an October 2026 flood in Tuscany, no cells stood out on the preceding pass, while 3.5% of the analysed cells stood out three days later and 2.8% on the following pass. Where both polarisations exist, the app explains what their changes may indicate, always labelling possible causes as hypotheses.

We evaluated the detector by injecting changes of known size into real observations. On quiet ground, it detected a 6 dB drop over a 2.5 km patch 98 times in 100; without injected changes, 0.06% of cells were flagged. Performance was weaker on seasonally changing ground: a 3 dB drop was detected only 33 times in 100. These controlled tests are not presented as proof of real-world disaster-detection accuracy. A separate prediction tool evaluates the next radar reading against simple baselines.

3. BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
Radar can observe through clouds, smoke and darkness, but interpreting its images requires expertise. Our app makes this evidence accessible to students, agricultural advisers, environmental researchers and people investigating disaster impacts. It shows where unusual radar changes occurred, with the observations and sources available for inspection.

A longer observation history and further validation could help identify areas worth investigating after events or during agricultural seasons. The current app is a research and educational prototype, not an operational warning service.

4. TOOLS
We used JavaScript ES modules, GLSL, HTML, CSS and three.js with a custom tile and terrain engine; satellite.js for orbit calculations; and Python with earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, pyproj and Pillow for measurements. Automated tests and Playwright support verification. GitHub Actions runs scheduled processing, while GitHub Pages and Cloudflare host the website. Visitors need no login, API key or installation; background measurements use Earthdata authentication.

5. WHAT IS CREATIVE
The project connects a global radar mosaic with local, inspectable evidence. Users can move from an event to its satellite timeline, calibrated measurements and possible explanations in one interface. It combines a mosaic assembled from 48 days of observations, interactive change maps, agricultural time series, side-by-side L-band and C-band imagery, and NISAR’s calculated live position and estimated next pass.

6. WHAT WE CONSIDERED
We prioritised accuracy, accessibility, transparency and performance. Preview imagery is distinguished from calibrated measurements, sources are linked, and illustrative animations are labelled. NISAR’s short observation history and seasonal variability limit interpretation: a detected difference does not establish its cause, and no detected difference does not prove that no damage occurred.

An AI coding assistant supported development under the team’s direction. The browser app does not call an AI model; its explanations use data-filled templates and explicit rules.
